Supply chain: something the app relies on, like an add-on or library, goes bad (fix: check and update what you rely on). Perfect code alone doesn't make a system safe."
language: maths

**Your mission:** other clubs' apps have had incidents. Learn from them, then check the Coding Club's app for the same kinds of weakness before anything goes wrong.

## Engage: whose fault?

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing to whether bug-free code is enough tests the new move: weaknesses also come from people and from what an app relies on."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "A club's programmers test every line of their app's code and find no bugs. Is the app safe?"
  options: ["Not necessarily: people and the add-ons it relies on can still be weak", "Yes: no bugs means no way in", "Only if it has a padlock", "Yes, until it gets more members"]
  actual: "Not necessarily. A shared password or a bad add-on lets someone in however good the club's own code is."
```

## Explore: three incidents

```step
stage: run
insight: "Students sort three incidents by where the weakness was and find the three kinds by contrast."
try: { playground: board, starter: "cyber.yml#explore", height: 560 }
check: { type: board, text: "Where was each weakness: in the app's own code, in what a person did, or in something the app relies on?", when: "t = n", explain: "The missed update is software, the password given away is user, the changed add-on is supply chain." }
```

Was your prediction right?

## Explain: three kinds

```step
stage: investigate
insight: "The teacher models naming the kind and its fix for each incident. Sam trusts bug-free code, the misconception planted after the method."
check:
  type: bug
  code: "working.txt#sam"
  text: "Sam's team checks their app. Click the line where it first goes wrong."
  answer: 3
  fault: logic
  misconception: good-code-is-safe
  explain: "Line 3: their own code is only one kind of weakness. People and add-ons can still let someone in, so they still need MFA and updates."
```

```worked
\text{Software} :: A flaw in the app's own code, such as never checking what is typed. Fix: test it and install updates.
\text{User} :: What people do: weak, shared or reused passwords, or being tricked. Fix: training, strong passwords, MFA.
\text{Supply chain} :: Something the app relies on (an add-on, a library) is out of date, taken over or a lookalike. Fix: check and update what you rely on.
\text{why it matters} :: Each kind is a different way in, so each needs its own fix.
```

### Find the mistake

## Elaborate: six incidents

```step
stage: modify
insight: "One change: more incidents, and now the fix as well as the kind."
try: { playground: board, starter: "cyber.yml#elaborate", height: 760 }
check: { type: board, text: "Sort all six incidents and choose the fix that would have stopped each one.", when: "t = n and f = n", explain: "Software: the missed update and the unchecked long name. User: the phone call and password1. Supply chain: the changed add-on and the lookalike library name." }
```

## Elaborate: our own app

```step
stage: make
insight: "Applying the kinds to a new system: the club's own app, before anything has gone wrong."
try: { playground: board, starter: "cyber.yml#make", height: 560 }
hint: ["Is the problem in the club's own code, in what people do, or in something the app relies on?", "Each kind has its own fix."]
check: { type: board, text: "Your review of the club app found three weaknesses. Name each kind and its fix.", when: "t = n and f = n", explain: "Unchecked input is software, the shared sticky-note password is user, the unchecked add-on is supply chain. Fixing them now is cheaper than after an incident." }
```

## Elaborate: an AI model is part of the supply chain

```step
stage: modify
tier: typical
insight: "The same supply chain idea, one new kind of part: an AI model file someone else made."
check:
  type: question
  q: "The club downloads a free AI model from a model-sharing website to sort members' photos. Opening the file quietly runs code that sends the photos somewhere else. What kind of weakness is it, and what's the fix?"
  options: ["Supply chain: only load models from makers you trust, and check them like any program", "Software: rewrite the club's own code", "User: tell members to stop uploading photos", "None: AI models are just data"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "The club's own code was fine. The problem came in with something it relied on.", "Members did nothing wrong.", "Some model files can run code when they are opened, so treat them like programs."]
  explain: "A model file the app relies on is part of the supply chain. Security researchers found about 100 malicious models on one popular model-sharing site in 2024."
```

AI apps rely on **models** other people trained, often downloaded from model-sharing websites. Some model files can **run code when they're opened**. In 2024, researchers found about **100 malicious models** on one popular site: opening one could let an attacker run their own code on the computer.

So an AI model is part of the **supply chain**: treat a model file like a program. Use models from makers you trust, check them, and keep them up to date.

## Evaluate: look back

```step
stage: info
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "A school app uses a free maps library. The library's makers stop updating it. What kind of weakness is growing?"
      options: ["Supply chain", "User", "Software, in the school's own code", "None, if it still works"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "No person did anything wrong.", "The school's own code hasn't changed.", "Flaws found later won't be fixed."]
      explain: "The app relies on it. Replace it with a maintained one, or plan to."
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "I can name the three kinds of weakness and a fix for each." }
```

### Look back

```teacher
summary: Students sort incidents at fictional club apps into software, user and
  supply-chain weaknesses with the fix for each, then review the Coding Club's
  own app (AC9TDI10P13 node 2). Descriptive and defensive throughout. A 5E
  mission lesson.
time: 45
timing: Engage and Explore 10 min · Explain 10 min · Elaborate 18 min · Evaluate 7 min
goals:
  - I can describe software, user and supply-chain weaknesses.
  - I can match each kind to a fix.
  - I can spot each kind in a system before it goes wrong.
struggle: "Students call every incident software because it happened in an app.
  Ask: whose action, or whose code, was the weak part?"
before: |
  AI step (typical, added 18 Oct 2026): an AI model file as part of the supply chain. Source (checked 18 Oct 2026, AI society research brief claim 54): JFrog, 27 Feb 2024, about 100 malicious models on Hugging Face; loading one can "run arbitrary code on the machine that loads or runs the model". https://jfrog.com/blog/data-scientists-targeted-by-malicious-hugging-face-ml-models-with-silent-backdoor/. Plain idea: opening an untrusted model is like running an untrusted program. Defensive and conceptual only.
  Try the board yourself. The clubs and incidents are made up.

  The one idea: weaknesses come from the app's own code, from people, and from what the app relies on; each needs its own fix.

  This lesson stays descriptive and defensive: what each kind is and how it is fixed. Node 3 (exploring a vulnerability in the student's own software) is left to class, with the teacher, on the students' own projects.

  Wider: news reports of real breaches can be sorted into the three kinds. Choose the reports yourself.
running:
  - "Engage: ask who was at fault in each of the hook's three stories."
  - "Explore: ask which incident was hardest to place, and why."
  - "Explain: model naming the kind and the fix for one incident."
  - "Elaborate: ask why the lookalike library name is supply chain and not user."
  - "Evaluate: discuss what the school should do about the old maps library."
stuck:
  - see: A student thinks bug-free code means safe (Sam's mistake).
    ask: Could a shared password let someone in, even with perfect code?
    fix: Code is one kind of weakness of three.
  - see: A student puts the lookalike library under User.
    ask: What did the app end up relying on?
    fix: "Something it relies on went bad: supply chain."
stretch: Find a news report of a real breach and sort its causes into the three kinds.
support: A card with the three kinds, an example and a fix for each.
leads: |
  Next: The Australian Privacy Principles.
exit:
  q: Name the three kinds of weakness with one fix for each.
  a: Software (test and update the code), user (training, strong passwords, MFA),
    supply chain (check and update what you rely on).
explain: >
  Systems have three kinds of **weakness**:


  - **Software:** a flaw in the app's own code. Fix: test it and install
  updates.

  - **User:** what people do (weak or shared passwords, being tricked). Fix:
  training, strong passwords, MFA.

  - **Supply chain:** something the app relies on goes bad. Fix: check and
  update what you rely on.


  Perfect code alone doesn't make a system safe.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: A team tests every line of its code and finds no bugs. Is the app safe?
    prompts:
      - What isn't in their code?
      - Who else touches the app?
    notes: People, settings and add-ons count too. Keep it conceptual.
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: activity
      title: Beyond the code
      minutes: 5
      do: |
        Pairs list ways into an app that aren't a bug in its own code.
      notes: Shared passwords, old add-ons, default settings, a person tricked.
        Compare lists.
    - at: modify
      kind: discussion
      title: Sort the weaknesses
      minutes: 3
      do: >
        Sort your list into: the team's code, other people's code, settings,
        people.
      notes: Each needs a different kind of fix.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Kinds of weakness
      type: question
      q: Which is a weakness that isn't a bug in the club's own code?
      options:
        - A shared password
        - A typo in a comment
        - A slow page
        - The wrong colour
      answer: 0
      explain: People and add-ons can let someone in however good the code is.
```
